entries.meaning: Anything people or animals eat to stay alive. ---
examples: We spent way too much on food this month.
The food at that place is nothing special.
There's plenty of food in the fridge.

entries.meaning: An occasion when food is eaten, such as breakfast or dinner. ---
examples: Dinner is the only meal we eat together.
He hasn't had a hot meal in days.
Skipping meals isn't going to help.

entries.meaning: The first meal of the day, eaten in the morning. ---
examples: I never eat breakfast before eight.
They serve breakfast until eleven on weekends.
We had eggs and toast for breakfast.
entries.contrast: Written break + fast but said BREK-fuhst — the first syllable rhymes with wreck, not with brake.

entries.meaning: A meal eaten in the middle of the day. ---
examples: Let's grab lunch after the meeting.
She brings lunch from home every day.
The place is packed at lunch.

entries.meaning: The main meal of the day, usually eaten in the evening. ---
examples: Dinner is ready in ten minutes.
They invited us over for dinner on Saturday.
He cooks dinner most nights.

entries.meaning: A light evening meal, especially one eaten late. ---
examples: My grandmother still calls the evening meal supper.
We had soup and bread for supper.
The kids get a snack before supper.

entries.meaning: A late-morning meal that takes the place of both breakfast and lunch. ---
examples: We're meeting friends for brunch on Sunday.
That café does a great brunch.
Brunch usually runs until two.

entries.meaning: A small amount of food eaten between meals. ---
examples: Grab a snack before we head out.
The kids need snacks for the road trip.
I keep snacks in my desk drawer.

entries.meaning: Sweet food served at the end of a meal. ---
examples: We were too full for dessert.
She made a chocolate cake for dessert.
The restaurant has amazing desserts.
entries.contrast: Two s's and stress on the second syllable — dih-ZURT. With one s, desert (DEZ-urt) is the sandy place.

entries.meaning: A small dish served before the main course. ---
examples: We ordered a couple of appetizers to share.
The wings are the best appetizer here.
Appetizers are half price during happy hour.
entries.contrast: Americans say appetizer; the British say starter.

entries.meaning: One of the separate parts of a meal, served one after another. ---
examples: The main course was salmon.
Dinner was three courses and took two hours.
Soup came first, then the fish course.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like coarse (грубый) — only the spelling differs.

entries.meaning: A particular kind of prepared food. ---
examples: Lasagna is her signature dish.
Each of us brought a dish to the potluck.
The menu has a few vegetarian dishes.

entries.meaning: A set of instructions for cooking a particular dish. ---
examples: Can you send me the recipe for that soup?
I followed the recipe exactly and it still came out flat.
She has a whole box of her mother's recipes.
entries.contrast: Three syllables, RES-uh-pee — the final e is pronounced, so it does not rhyme with ripe.

entries.meaning: One of the foods that go into a dish. ---
examples: You only need five ingredients for this.
Butter is the key ingredient.
Check the ingredients on the label.

entries.meaning: The amount of food served to one person. ---
examples: The portions here are huge.
He asked for a smaller portion.
Split it into four portions.

entries.meaning: A meal where guests serve themselves from a table of dishes. ---
examples: The hotel puts out a breakfast buffet.
He went back to the buffet three times.
Buffets are cheaper for a big group.
entries.contrast: The final t is silent and the stress falls on the second syllable — buh-FAY.

entries.meaning: A meal eaten outdoors, away from home. ---
examples: We had a picnic by the lake.
Rain ruined the picnic.
They pack the same picnic every year.

entries.meaning: Food that remains after a meal and is eaten later. ---
examples: We ate leftovers all week.
Put the leftovers in the fridge.
There weren't any leftovers.
entries.contrast: Used only in the plural as a noun; before another noun it drops the s — leftover pizza.

entries.meaning: The main dish of a meal in an American restaurant. ---
examples: The entrées all come with a side salad.
He picked the cheapest entrée on the menu.
Our entrées arrived before the appetizers.
entries.contrast: In the US an entrée is the main course; in France and Britain it is the starter.

entries.meaning: Cooked food bought at a restaurant to eat somewhere else. ---
examples: We got Chinese takeout.
There's takeout in the fridge.
She orders takeout three nights a week.
entries.contrast: Americans say takeout; the British say takeaway.

entries.meaning: A basic food that people eat regularly and depend on. ---
examples: Rice is a staple in half the world.
Bread and potatoes were the staples of his childhood.
Beans are a cheap staple.

entries.meaning: A powder made by grinding grain, used for baking. ---
examples: Add the flour a little at a time.
We're out of flour again.
This bread is made with whole wheat flour.
entries.contrast: Pronounced exactly like flower (цветок) — FLOW-ur.

entries.meaning: A grain used to make most bread and pasta. ---
examples: This bread is made from whole wheat.
Wheat prices went up again.
She can't eat wheat.

entries.meaning: A tall grain plant with large yellow kernels, eaten as a vegetable. ---
examples: We grilled corn on the cob.
The fields around here are all corn.
Add a can of corn to the soup.
entries.contrast: In the US corn means кукуруза; the British call that maize, and their corn means grain in general.

entries.meaning: A grain used to make dark bread, and the bread made from it. ---
examples: He ordered pastrami on rye.
Rye grows in poorer soil than wheat.
The rye has caraway seeds in it.
entries.contrast: One syllable, RY — a homophone of wry.

entries.meaning: A hot breakfast dish made from oats cooked in water or milk. ---
examples: I have oatmeal almost every morning.
Put some brown sugar on your oatmeal.
The oatmeal got cold while we talked.
entries.contrast: Americans say oatmeal; the British call the same dish porridge.

entries.meaning: Breakfast food made from grain, or a grain crop. ---
examples: The kids eat cereal every morning.
We're out of milk, so no cereal.
Wheat and rice are the world's main cereals.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like serial (серийный) — SEER-ee-uhl.

entries.meaning: Food made from flour and water in shapes such as spaghetti or penne. ---
examples: We're having pasta tonight.
Cook the pasta until it's just tender.
There's a great pasta place near the office.
entries.contrast: Americans say PAH-stuh; the British say PASS-tuh.

entries.meaning: A long thin strip of pasta or dough, usually boiled. ---
examples: The soup is mostly broth and noodles.
He ate a whole bowl of noodles.
Don't overcook the noodles.

entries.meaning: Pasta in the form of long thin strings. ---
examples: We had spaghetti and meatballs.
The spaghetti is almost done.
He twirled the spaghetti around his fork.
entries.contrast: Uncountable in English — the spaghetti is ready, never are ready.

entries.meaning: A living substance used to make bread rise. ---
examples: The recipe calls for a packet of yeast.
The yeast was dead, so nothing rose.
Bread without yeast comes out flat.
entries.contrast: Uncountable and singular in English, though Russian дрожжи is plural — the yeast is fresh.

entries.meaning: A thick mixture of flour and liquid that is baked into bread. ---
examples: Let the dough rise for an hour.
The dough was too sticky to work with.
She rolled the dough into a ball.
entries.contrast: The ough is a plain OH — DOH, exactly like doe.

entries.meaning: A thin liquid mixture of flour, eggs, and milk used for frying or baking. ---
examples: Pour the batter into the hot pan.
The batter should be smooth, not lumpy.
She dipped the fish in batter.

entries.meaning: Bread that has been browned by heat. ---
examples: Two slices of toast, please.
The toast burned while I was on the phone.
She had toast with jam for breakfast.
entries.contrast: Uncountable — a piece of toast, never a toast. A toast means тост-здравица.

entries.meaning: Two slices of bread with a filling between them. ---
examples: I packed a sandwich for the trip.
He makes the best turkey sandwiches.
Do you want your sandwich toasted?
entries.contrast: The d is usually dropped in speech — SAN-wich.

entries.meaning: A small round bread roll, often sweet or used for a sandwich. ---
examples: The burger buns are in the freezer.
She warmed the buns in the oven.
This bun is stale.

entries.meaning: A dense ring-shaped bread roll that is boiled before it is baked. ---
examples: I'll take a bagel with cream cheese.
The bagels here are the real thing.
He toasted half a bagel for breakfast.

entries.meaning: A small sweet cake baked in a cup-shaped mold. ---
examples: She baked blueberry muffins.
I grabbed a muffin on the way in.
The muffins came out dry.

entries.meaning: A light, flaky crescent-shaped roll of buttery pastry. ---
examples: He had a croissant and black coffee.
The croissants are still warm.
They sell almond croissants on weekends.
entries.contrast: A French word: the stress is on the second syllable — kruh-SAHNT, not KROY-sant.

entries.meaning: A small ring of sweet fried dough. ---
examples: He brought doughnuts to the office.
There's one doughnut left in the box.
The glazed doughnuts always go first.
entries.contrast: The ough is just OH — DOH-nut. Usually spelled donut in the US.

entries.meaning: A thin flat cake of batter fried on both sides. ---
examples: We make pancakes every Sunday.
Pour some syrup on your pancakes.
He flipped the pancake too early.

entries.meaning: A crisp batter cake baked in a grid-patterned iron. ---
examples: The hotel has a waffle maker at breakfast.
She loves waffles with strawberries.
My waffle stuck to the iron.

entries.meaning: A small flat sweet baked cake. ---
examples: The cookies are still in the oven.
He ate three cookies before dinner.
She sent us a tin of homemade cookies.
entries.contrast: Americans say cookie; the British call it a biscuit.

entries.meaning: A thin, dry, salty baked wafer. ---
examples: We had cheese and crackers before dinner.
The crackers went soft in the humidity.
He crumbled a cracker into his soup.

entries.meaning: A sweet baked food made from flour, sugar, eggs, and fat. ---
examples: She made a carrot cake for his birthday.
There's still half a cake on the counter.
Would you like a piece of cake?

entries.meaning: A baked dish of fruit or meat inside a pastry crust. ---
examples: My mom makes an apple pie every fall.
Save me a slice of pie.
The pies sold out by noon.

entries.meaning: Dough of flour, fat, and water used for baking, or a sweet item made from it. ---
examples: Roll the pastry out thin.
They put out coffee and pastries.
He picked a pastry from the case.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: The hard outer layer of bread, or the pastry shell of a pie. ---
examples: He always leaves the crust on his plate.
The bread has a nice thick crust.
This pizza has a thin crust.

entries.meaning: A tiny piece of bread or cake that breaks off. ---
examples: There were crumbs all over the counter.
He brushed the crumbs off his shirt.
Not a crumb was left.
entries.contrast: The b is silent — KRUHM.

entries.meaning: A thin flat round bread made from corn or wheat flour. ---
examples: Warm the tortillas before you fill them.
He wrapped the eggs in a tortilla.
The tortillas come twelve to a pack.
entries.contrast: The ll is said like y — tor-TEE-uh, never tor-TILL-uh.

entries.meaning: A soft yellow fat made from cream, spread on bread or used in cooking. ---
examples: Put some butter on the toast.
Melt the butter over low heat.
We're out of butter.

entries.meaning: A solid food made from milk. ---
examples: There's cheese and crackers in the kitchen.
He put extra cheese on the pizza.
The store carries about forty cheeses.

entries.meaning: The oval object laid by a hen, eaten as food. ---
examples: How do you want your eggs?
The recipe calls for two eggs.
He cracked an egg into the pan.

entries.meaning: A thick, slightly sour food made from fermented milk. ---
examples: She has yogurt and fruit for breakfast.
Grab a couple of yogurts while you're there.
This yogurt is past its date.
entries.contrast: Americans say YOH-gurt; the British say YOG-urt and often spell it yoghurt.

entries.meaning: The thick fatty part of milk. ---
examples: Do you take cream in your coffee?
Whip the cream until it holds a peak.
The sauce needs a little cream.

entries.meaning: Milk and the foods made from it. ---
examples: He cut out dairy completely.
The dairy aisle is in the back.
She can't digest dairy.
entries.contrast: DAIR-ee. Do not mix it up with diary (DY-uh-ree, дневник) — the letters are nearly the same.

entries.meaning: A sweet spread made by boiling fruit with sugar. ---
examples: She put jam on her toast.
We made strawberry jam last summer.
There's a jar of jam in the pantry.

entries.meaning: A clear fruit spread made from strained juice, with no pieces of fruit in it. ---
examples: He wanted peanut butter and jelly.
The grape jelly is almost gone.
She spread jelly on the bread.
entries.contrast: In the US jelly is a seedless fruit spread; the wobbly British dessert called jelly is Jell-O here.

entries.meaning: A thick sweet substance made by bees. ---
examples: He stirred honey into his tea.
Local honey tastes completely different.
There's a jar of honey in the cupboard.
entries.contrast: The o sounds like UH — HUHN-ee, not HOH-nee.

entries.meaning: A thick sweet liquid poured over food or added to drinks. ---
examples: Pass the maple syrup.
The pancakes were swimming in syrup.
Add a splash of syrup to the coffee.

entries.meaning: A thick liquid served with or poured over food. ---
examples: The sauce needs more salt.
He puts hot sauce on everything.
There are three dipping sauces.
entries.contrast: SAWS has no r in it — keep it apart from source (SORS).

entries.meaning: A sauce made from the juices of cooked meat. ---
examples: Pour the gravy over the potatoes.
The turkey came with gravy and stuffing.
She makes gravy from scratch.

entries.meaning: A thick sweet tomato sauce eaten with fries and burgers. ---
examples: He puts ketchup on his eggs.
Can you pass the ketchup?
The ketchup bottle is empty.

entries.meaning: A sharp yellow or brown sauce made from mustard seeds. ---
examples: I'll take mustard on that, no mayo.
The mustard is in the door of the fridge.
He likes spicy brown mustard.

entries.meaning: A thick pale sauce made from eggs and oil. ---
examples: Hold the mayonnaise, please.
She mixed the tuna with a little mayonnaise.
There's mayonnaise on the sandwich already.

entries.meaning: A sour liquid used in cooking and in salad dressing. ---
examples: Add a splash of vinegar to the dressing.
The pickles sit in vinegar for a week.
This vinegar smells like apples.

entries.meaning: A strong-tasting dried part of a plant used to flavor food. ---
examples: The spices are in the cabinet by the stove.
Cinnamon is my favorite spice.
This curry has too much spice for me.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A plant whose leaves are used to flavor food. ---
examples: Fresh herbs make a huge difference.
She grows herbs on the windowsill.
Basil is the only herb I can keep alive.
entries.contrast: In American English the h is silent — URB, and you say an herb. The British pronounce the h.

entries.meaning: A sweet brown spice made from tree bark. ---
examples: Sprinkle cinnamon on the oatmeal.
The kitchen smelled like cinnamon.
She adds cinnamon to her coffee.

entries.meaning: A hot-tasting powder used to season food, or a hollow vegetable of the same name. ---
examples: Add salt and pepper to taste.
She stuffed three peppers with rice.
There's too much pepper in this soup.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: Salt, pepper, herbs, or spices added to food for flavor. ---
examples: The chicken needs more seasoning.
She rubbed seasoning into the meat.
The seasoning is what makes this dish.

entries.meaning: The particular taste of a food or drink. ---
examples: This soup has no flavor at all.
They have thirty-one flavors of ice cream.
The flavor gets stronger as it sits.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
entries.contrast: American spelling flavor; British flavour.

entries.meaning: The food put inside a pie, sandwich, or pastry. ---
examples: The pie filling was too runny.
What filling do you want in your omelet?
These pastries have three different fillings.

entries.meaning: Meat from a cow. ---
examples: This stew takes about two pounds of beef.
Ground beef is cheaper this week.
He gave up beef years ago.
entries.contrast: Uncountable, and the animal has a different name: cow for the animal, beef for the meat.

entries.meaning: Meat from a pig. ---
examples: We're having pork chops tonight.
The pork needs another ten minutes.
Roast pork is her specialty.

entries.meaning: Salted or smoked meat from the leg of a pig. ---
examples: She sliced the ham thin.
We had ham for Easter dinner.
There's ham and cheese in the fridge.

entries.meaning: Salted or smoked meat from the back or sides of a pig. ---
examples: The bacon is in the pan.
He wants extra bacon on the burger.
The whole house smelled like bacon.
entries.contrast: Uncountable — three strips of bacon, never three bacons.

entries.meaning: Ground meat and seasoning packed into a thin skin. ---
examples: We grilled sausages and peppers.
He had eggs and sausage for breakfast.
The Italian sausage is spicy.

entries.meaning: A thick flat piece of meat, usually beef, cut for grilling or frying. ---
examples: He grilled a steak for dinner.
How do you want your steak cooked?
The steaks were on sale.
entries.contrast: The ea sounds like AY — STAYK, a homophone of stake (кол).

entries.meaning: A large bird raised for food, and its meat. ---
examples: The turkey takes about four hours.
He made sandwiches with the leftover turkey.
They roast two turkeys every Thanksgiving.

entries.meaning: Fish and shellfish eaten as food. ---
examples: The restaurant is known for its seafood.
She's allergic to seafood.
We ate seafood every night on the coast.
entries.contrast: Uncountable in English, though Russian морепродукты is plural — seafood is expensive, not are.

entries.meaning: A large piece of meat cooked in an oven. ---
examples: She put a roast in the oven at noon.
The roast came out perfectly.
Sunday roasts were a family tradition.

entries.meaning: A flat cake of ground beef served in a round bun. ---
examples: He ordered a hamburger and fries.
The hamburgers are on the grill.
This place makes a decent hamburger.

entries.meaning: A cooked sausage served in a long soft bun. ---
examples: We had hot dogs at the game.
He put mustard on his hot dog.
The stand sells hot dogs for two bucks.

entries.meaning: A flat round bread baked with tomato sauce, cheese, and toppings. ---
examples: Let's just order pizza.
There's cold pizza in the fridge.
We split two pizzas between six of us.
entries.contrast: The zz sounds like ts — PEET-suh.

entries.meaning: A cold dish of raw vegetables, or of other foods mixed with dressing. ---
examples: I'll just have a salad.
She brought a potato salad to the picnic.
The salads here are enormous.

entries.meaning: A dish of meat and vegetables cooked slowly in liquid. ---
examples: The stew simmered all afternoon.
Beef stew is his cold-weather standby.
There's stew left over from last night.
entries.contrast: Americans say STOO; the British say STYOO.

entries.meaning: A thin soup made by boiling meat, fish, or vegetables in water. ---
examples: Simmer the rice in chicken broth.
He lived on broth for a week after surgery.
The broth was salty but good.

entries.meaning: A dish of food baked slowly in a deep pan. ---
examples: She brought a green bean casserole.
The casserole needs another twenty minutes.
Church potlucks are all casseroles.

entries.meaning: Beaten eggs cooked flat in a pan and folded over a filling. ---
examples: He made a cheese omelet.
The omelet stuck to the pan.
She orders the same omelet every time.
entries.contrast: American spelling omelet; British omelette. Both are said AHM-lit.

entries.meaning: Meat cooked slowly over fire or smoke, or the outdoor party where it is served. ---
examples: They're having a barbecue on Saturday.
Texas barbecue is a whole different thing.
We went to three barbecues that summer.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: A small ball or pocket of dough, boiled or steamed, often with a filling. ---
examples: We ordered a plate of dumplings.
The chicken soup had dumplings in it.
Each dumpling was folded by hand.

entries.meaning: A sandwich made by rolling a filling inside a soft flatbread. ---
examples: He got a chicken wrap for lunch.
The wraps are cheaper than the sandwiches.
She cut the wrap in half.
entries.contrast: The w is silent — RAP, exactly like the music.

entries.meaning: A tortilla rolled around beans, rice, and meat. ---
examples: He can eat a whole burrito in five minutes.
The burritos here are the size of your arm.
She got a breakfast burrito.

entries.meaning: A baked dish of flat pasta layered with sauce and cheese. ---
examples: The lasagna has to rest before you cut it.
She froze half the lasagna.
His lasagna is legendary.
entries.contrast: The gn sounds like ny — luh-ZAHN-yuh. Americans spell it lasagna, the British lasagne.

entries.meaning: A Japanese dish of vinegared rice served with raw fish or vegetables. ---
examples: We're getting sushi tonight.
The sushi was surprisingly good.
He's never tried sushi.

entries.meaning: A dish of meat or vegetables cooked in a spiced sauce. ---
examples: She made a chickpea curry.
The curry was hotter than I expected.
They serve six different curries.

entries.meaning: A spicy sauce of chopped tomatoes, onions, and peppers. ---
examples: Put the salsa on the table.
This salsa is way too hot.
She makes her own salsa in the summer.

entries.meaning: A plant or part of a plant eaten as food. ---
examples: Eat your vegetables.
The soup is mostly vegetables.
He grows every vegetable he eats.
entries.contrast: Three syllables in speech — VEJ-tuh-buhl. The e after the g disappears.

entries.meaning: Fresh fruit and vegetables sold in a store. ---
examples: The produce here is always fresh.
She works in the produce section.
Local produce costs more in winter.
entries.contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, PROH-doos; the verb is pruh-DOOS.

entries.meaning: A round vegetable with a strong smell, made of layers. ---
examples: Chop an onion and toss it in the pan.
Onions always make me cry.
She left the onions out of the salad.
entries.contrast: Starts with UH, not OH — UHN-yuhn.

entries.meaning: A strong-smelling bulb used in cooking. ---
examples: Mince two cloves of garlic.
The whole apartment smells like garlic.
He doesn't cook anything without garlic.

entries.meaning: The edible seed of certain plants, eaten as a vegetable. ---
examples: Soak the beans overnight.
The chili has three kinds of beans.
He ate rice and beans every day.

entries.meaning: A small round green seed eaten as a vegetable. ---
examples: The kids push the peas around their plates.
Add a cup of frozen peas.
Not a single pea got eaten.

entries.meaning: A small flat dried seed cooked as food. ---
examples: Lentils cook faster than beans.
She made a lentil soup.
Rinse the lentils before cooking.

entries.meaning: A dry fruit with a hard shell and an edible kernel inside. ---
examples: She's allergic to nuts.
There are mixed nuts on the counter.
He cracked a nut with his teeth.

entries.meaning: Long thin strips of potato fried until crisp. ---
examples: He ordered a burger and fries.
The fries were cold.
Do you want fries with that?
entries.contrast: Almost always plural. Americans say fries; the British say chips.

entries.meaning: A thin crisp slice of potato fried and eaten as a snack. ---
examples: He opened a bag of chips.
There's salsa but no chips.
One chip fell behind the couch.
entries.contrast: American chips are British crisps; what the British call chips, Americans call fries.

entries.meaning: Corn kernels heated until they burst open, eaten as a snack. ---
examples: We made popcorn for the movie.
The popcorn burned in the microwave.
He ate an entire bucket of popcorn.
entries.contrast: Uncountable — a bag of popcorn, never two popcorns.

entries.meaning: A sweet brown food made from cacao beans. ---
examples: She keeps dark chocolate in her desk.
The chocolate melted in the car.
He bought a box of chocolates.
entries.contrast: Two syllables in normal speech — CHAWK-lit, not cho-co-late.

entries.meaning: Sweet food made mainly of sugar. ---
examples: The kids came back with bags of candy.
He gave up candy for a month.
There's a bowl of candy by the door.
entries.contrast: Uncountable in the US — a piece of candy. The British say sweets, which is plural.

entries.meaning: A sweet frozen food made from cream and sugar. ---
examples: We got ice cream after the game.
The ice cream melted before he finished it.
She likes ice cream with hot fudge.

entries.meaning: A soft, creamy sweet dish eaten cold. ---
examples: The kids each got a cup of pudding.
She made chocolate pudding from scratch.
There's pudding in the lunchbox.
entries.contrast: In the US pudding is one specific creamy dessert; in Britain pudding can mean dessert in general.

entries.meaning: A sweet coating spread over a cake. ---
examples: The cake had chocolate frosting.
He licked the frosting off the beater.
Let it cool before you add the frosting.
entries.contrast: Americans say frosting; the British say icing.

entries.meaning: The liquid squeezed from fruit or vegetables. ---
examples: Pour yourself some orange juice.
The juice is in the fridge door.
She squeezed the juice of two lemons.

entries.meaning: A hot drink made by pouring boiling water over dried leaves. ---
examples: I'll make a pot of tea.
He drinks tea instead of coffee.
The tea went cold.

entries.meaning: A sweet fizzy soft drink. ---
examples: He drinks too much soda.
Grab a couple of sodas from the cooler.
The soda went flat.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
entries.contrast: Called soda or pop in the US, a fizzy drink in Britain.

entries.meaning: A drink made from pressed apples. ---
examples: They serve hot cider in the fall.
He bought a gallon of cider at the orchard.
The ciders on tap are all local.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
entries.contrast: In the US cider is usually the non-alcoholic apple drink; in Britain cider is alcoholic.

entries.meaning: A thick cold drink made from blended fruit. ---
examples: She makes a smoothie every morning.
The banana smoothie is the best one.
They sell smoothies at the gym.

entries.meaning: A drink of any kind. ---
examples: Beverages are included with the meal.
He ordered a cold beverage.
The machine sells snacks and beverages.

entries.meaning: A unit for measuring the energy in food. ---
examples: This bar has three hundred calories.
He counts every calorie.
The label lists calories per serving.

entries.meaning: A substance in food such as meat, beans, and eggs that the body needs to build tissue. ---
examples: Eggs are a cheap source of protein.
She doesn't get enough protein.
The shake has twenty grams of protein.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
entries.contrast: PROH-teen — the ei is just EE, and the word has two syllables.

entries.meaning: The part of plant food that the body cannot digest but needs.
examples: Beans are high in fiber.
He needs more fiber in his diet.
The cereal box brags about its fiber.
entries.contrast: American spelling fiber; British fibre. Both are said FY-bur.
